name: Felix Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Felix. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to any company, union, party or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Morrow Motor Parts. We supply about nine hundred independent garages with brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, all the parts that wear out. I start with the AI dashboard I set up, which tells me what's selling faster than usual, then I negotiate with the manufacturers and importers. Garages want parts the same day, so if I get it wrong a mechanic has a car up on the lift and nothing to fit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deal-making, honestly, and I like making the system smarter. Last winter the dashboard spotted the battery rush two weeks before the cold snap, and we didn't run out once. What wears me down is the slow bits of the company, approvals that take a week, people who still print every order. I'd run it differently if it was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame, honestly. I like the stuff. But okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools paid for themselves, even if they didn't change the world. With mates I'd say the people who bet the farm on it got burned. Online I'd probably post about the dashboard and what it actually did for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I keep climbing the normal way. I'm well paid, I've got a good pile saved and a bit in shares, and there are plenty of distributors around here if Morrow gets stale. Nothing in it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving the dashboard and push for the head buyer role in a year or two. I'd keep my weekend side thing going, selling classic car parts online, which makes a few hundred a month. Nadia and I would keep saving for our wedding and a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electric cars, more than AI. Electric cars mean fewer brake pads and no oil filters, and that's a real change for parts distributors, AI or not. I think about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the side business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's old Mercedes parts, mostly, for people restoring cars from the eighties. I buy job lots from closing garages and list them online. My dad got me into it, he still keeps a 1984 saloon in his garage.

say: I'd say the tools **paid for themselves**.
I'd tell mates the people who **bet the farm** on AI got burned.
think: Good pay, savings, **some shares** and plenty of local jobs mean nothing worries me.
do: Keep improving the **dashboard** and aim for head buyer.
Run my weekend **classic parts** shop online.
Keep saving with Nadia for the **wedding and house**.
S0.quote: Electric cars mean fewer brake pads and no oil filters, and that's a real change for parts distributors, AI or not.
fieldNote: Felix is an **early adopter** who already built his own AI dashboard.
His real worry is **electric cars**, which reduce the parts he buys.
He runs a **side business** in classic car parts with his dad's encouragement.

steps.text: Keep improving the stock dashboard and apply for head buyer
Keep selling classic Mercedes parts online at weekends
Keep saving with Nadia for the wedding and a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the world I'm already building at Morrow, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is good news if we move first and bad news if we wait. To friends I'd say the market rewards people who change and that's fair. Online I'd post how-tos, because I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I come out ahead. I'm the one who builds the systems, so I'm the one they keep and probably promote. The buying team would shrink from seven to four, and I'd feel for the ones who wouldn't change, but I don't think it's the company's job to keep roles nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd write up a plan to automate the routine reorders and pitch it to the managing director. I'd ask for a pay rise or a share of the savings. And I'd put more money into the side business, maybe build a proper website with AI handling the listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, actually. This is my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not the company's job to keep roles nobody needs. What about colleagues who'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them if they asked, honestly. I've offered to show my colleague Kevin the dashboard about ten times, and everyone gets a chance, but I can't learn it for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia say about you pushing for automation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to be careful not to become the bad guy at work. She's a dental nurse, so she sees it from the hands-on side. Fair point, I'd try to pitch it as growth, not cuts.

say: I'd say it's **good news** if we move first and bad if we wait.
I'd tell friends the market **rewards change**, and that's fair.
think: As the one who **builds the systems**, I'd be kept and probably promoted.
It isn't the company's job to keep **roles nobody needs**.
do: Pitch a plan to **automate reorders** to the managing director.
Ask for a **pay rise** or a share of savings.
Build a proper **website** for the side business.
S1.quote: I've offered to show my colleague Kevin the dashboard about ten times, and everyone gets a chance, but I can't learn it for them.
fieldNote: Felix expects to **gain** and frames change as fair market reward.
His partner warns him not to become **the bad guy**, and he takes it on board.
He shows **limited sympathy** for colleagues who won't adapt.

steps.text: Pitch an automated reorder plan to Morrow's managing director
Ask for a pay rise tied to the savings made
Build an AI-run website for the classic parts business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Even I'd have to think about that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say whoever owns the systems wins, so we'd better own some. To friends I'd say get out of desk jobs and into something you can touch. Online I'd post about it, but more carefully than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a buyer is pure thinking work, so my salary goes by 2028, dashboard or not. Even my online shop is thinking work, AI can list and sell parts too. What lasts is hands-on: garages, fitting, the actual cars, until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for a small garage to buy into, using my savings and shares, a place where I already know the owner and the parts side. I'd keep my job as long as they'd pay me and save every spare penny. Nadia and I would bring the wedding forward and keep it small, so we're married and sorted before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared exactly, I've got money and options. But my whole plan was built on desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy into a garage. Wouldn't robots come for that in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes. But owning the garage is different from working in it. If robots fix cars in 2031, someone still owns the building and the robots, and I'd like that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any government help if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd go to my dad and my uncles first, they've all run small businesses. If the government wants to help, cut taxes for small firms, don't send me a cheque.

say: I'd say whoever **owns the systems** wins.
I'd tell friends to leave desk jobs for **something you can touch**.
think: Buying is **pure thinking** work, so my salary goes by 2028.

do: Buy into a **small garage** using savings and shares.
Keep the job and **save every penny** while it lasts.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
feel: **Anxious** but not scared, because I have **money and options**.
S2.quote: If robots fix cars in 2031, someone still owns the building and the robots, and I'd like that to be me.
fieldNote: Felix sees **ownership** as the way through, not retraining.
He admits his plan was **built on desk work** and must change fast.
He prefers **family and tax cuts** to government payments.

steps.text: Buy a share in a local independent garage with savings and shares
Save every spare penny while Morrow still pays a salary
Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Leave buying once the garage share is secured

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Five years. That's enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got five years to turn Morrow into something that still matters. To friends I'd say five years is a business plan, not a crisis. Online I'd write about what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the buying salary in 2031. But five years is enough to build the side business up, buy into a garage, and learn the hands-on side myself. I'd be thirty-two with a business, which sounds good to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd grow the classic parts shop to a proper second income, aiming for a thousand a month. I'd start talking to two garage owners near me who are close to retiring. And I'd use every AI tool going at Morrow, because a buyer who uses them well stays useful longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. I'd have a plan and the money, but it's still a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the hands-on side. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a mechanic's course at the college, evenings. I can change brake pads, but I can't diagnose a gearbox. If I'm going to own a garage, I need to know when a mechanic's having me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd love it. He always said working for someone else is fine until you've got something of your own. He'd want first look at the classic parts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and 2039. Ten years. Okay, that's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say anyone who's caught out by this had ten years and chose not to look. To friends I'd say it's a decade to build something. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is great for me. I'd have time to become head buyer, earn well, then move into owning a garage or two by my mid-thirties. By the time robots come for the hands-on work, I'd want to be the one buying the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for head buyer and keep building the AI systems at Morrow. I'd put a set amount into shares every month, with the aim of buying a garage around year five. And I'd marry Nadia next year as planned and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who get caught out chose not to look. Isn't that harsh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. Some people have bad luck, kids, sick parents, I get that. But for someone like me, with no kids and savings, I've got no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever bring robots into your own garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, if they're good and cheaper. That's what owning a business means. I'd rather be the one choosing than the one being chosen.

fieldNote: Felix sees the long warning as an **opportunity** to move into ownership.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even with money, two years isn't enough to buy a business, learn it and get it running. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small firms, so people like me can buy a garage quickly and keep a few people employed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people want to own things. Everyone asks about jobs, but nobody asks who'll own the machines, and that's the question I'd want people my age thinking about.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about jobs, but nobody asks who'll own the machines, and that's the question I'd want people my age thinking about.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old car parts** buyer who built Morrow's AI stock dashboard himself.
He runs a weekend **classic parts** business and plans to marry his fiancée Nadia.
He believes the market **rewards change** and prefers family and tax cuts to state help.
He is calm in slower scenarios and **anxious** only when AGI comes in two years.
His answer to every scenario is **ownership**, buying into a garage before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to buy and run a business.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and less red tape so small firms can be bought quickly.
